lead: Above a safe cabin altitude the air holds too little oxygen for the body. The oxygen system raises the partial pressure of oxygen at the lungs by supplying stored gas, liquid oxygen, a chemical generator or, in military aircraft, on-board generation. It protects the crew during decompression and gives passengers time to descend. This chapter covers the need, the supply types, the regulator and mask parts, and the safety rules that keep oxygen from turning a small fire into a large one.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.6 for cabin altitude and Chapter 2.2 for bleed air.

sections.h3: Hypoxia and the need for oxygen

blocks.text: Hypoxia is a shortage of oxygen reaching the body tissues. It starts with headache and poor judgement, then leads to loss of consciousness. In an aircraft it is caused by low outside pressure: the fraction of oxygen in air stays near 0.21, but the total pressure falls, so the partial pressure of oxygen falls with it.

blocks.where: P<sub>O2</sub> is the partial pressure of oxygen in bar; F<sub>O2</sub> is the oxygen fraction (0.21 in air); P<sub>amb</sub> is ambient pressure in bar. At sea level P<sub>amb</sub> ≈ 1.013 bar gives P<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.213 bar. At 35,000 ft P<sub>amb</sub> ≈ 0.24 bar gives P<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.050 bar.

blocks.text: Cabin pressurisation keeps the cabin at a safe pressure altitude, often about 6,000 to 8,000 ft. If pressurisation fails, or if the cabin altitude is deliberately high, the crew needs supplemental oxygen. The time of useful consciousness (TUC) is the time from oxygen loss to inability to act. It falls from many minutes at 25,000 ft to about 30–60 s at 35,000 ft and 15–20 s at 40,000 ft. Oxygen systems must supply a mask within that time.

Stored or chemical oxygen raises F<sub>O2</sub> in the mask to nearly 1.0. This raises P<sub>O2</sub> at the lungs even when P<sub>amb</sub> is low. The system therefore buys time to descend to a safe cabin altitude.

Four supply types are common. High-pressure gaseous oxygen sits in cylinders at about 1,800 psi (124 bar). A filler valve fills the cylinder; a shut-off valve isolates it; a regulator reduces pressure; a mask delivers gas to the user. Liquid oxygen (LOX) stores more oxygen in less volume, but it must be kept cold and it boils off; it is used where weight and space matter. A chemical oxygen generator burns a sodium chlorate candle to release oxygen; it is simple and needs no pressure storage, but once started it cannot be stopped. Military aircraft often use an on-board oxygen generating system (OBOGS), which separates oxygen from engine bleed air with a molecular sieve.

Regulators come in three forms. A demand regulator opens only when the user inhales. A diluter-demand regulator mixes cabin air with oxygen at low altitude and goes to pure oxygen as cabin altitude rises. A pressure-demand regulator supplies oxygen above cabin pressure so the mask stays sealed and the lungs get oxygen even in a rapid decompression. Crew masks are usually pressure-demand; passenger masks are usually continuous-flow.

Other components are tubing, a pressure gauge, a mask and a relief valve. The gauge reads cylinder pressure, not the mass of gas left. To find gas quantity at constant temperature: V<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>w</sub> × P<sub>c</sub> ÷ P<sub>1</sub>. Here V<sub>w</sub> is cylinder water volume in L (the internal volume filled with water), P<sub>c</sub> is cylinder pressure in bar, P<sub>1</sub> is the pressure at which you want the volume (1 bar), and V<sub>1</sub> is gas volume at 1 bar.

Before flight the crew checks cylinder pressure and the mask seal. In flight the shut-off valve is open and the regulator is set to normal. The crew dons masks when cabin altitude passes the crew limit, often about 10,000 ft, and uses pressure-demand for smoke or rapid decompression. Passenger masks are in overhead panels. If cabin altitude rises above about 14,000 ft, the panels open automatically and the masks drop. The passenger pulls the mask to start flow; this is automatic mask drop-out. Portable cylinders are carried for walk-around use.

items: Check cylinder pressure and mask seal before flight.
Open the shut-off valve slowly and set the regulator to normal.
Don the mask when cabin altitude passes the crew limit, often about 10,000 ft.
If cabin altitude passes about 14,000 ft, passenger masks drop automatically; the passenger pulls to start flow.

blocks.text: Oxygen is not fuel, but it makes fuel and oil burn fiercely. Fittings must be cleaned for oxygen service; no grease, oil or PTFE tape on threads. Open cylinder valves slowly to avoid a pressure surge and adiabatic heating. Keep cylinders away from heat and secure them so they do not become missiles. A chemical generator becomes hot; do not cover it. A LOX converter vents oxygen; keep it away from ignition sources. In a fire, shut off supply if possible and use the fire procedure in Chapter 2.9.

examples.question: A passenger oxygen cylinder has a water volume of 50 L and is filled to 124 bar. Twelve passengers each draw 4 L/min at 1 bar. Ignore temperature change and regulator losses. How much gas at 1 bar is available, what is the total flow, and how long does the supply last?
steps: Gas available at 1 bar: V<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>w</sub> × P<sub>c</sub> ÷ P<sub>1</sub> = 50 L × 124 bar ÷ 1 bar = 6200 L.
Convert to hours: 129.166... min ÷ 60 = 2.153... h, about 2 h 9 min.
examples.answer: The cylinder holds 6200 L of gas at 1 bar, the total flow is 48 L/min, and the supply lasts 129 min, about 2 h 9 min.
examples.check:
v_w = 50.0
p_c = 124.0
p_1 = 1.0
n = 12
flow_each = 4.0
v1 = v_w * p_c / p_1
total_flow = n * flow_each
t = v1 / total_flow
print(v1)
print(total_flow)
print(t)

traps: Reading cylinder pressure as quantity: pressure must be multiplied by water volume, and pressure changes with temperature even when gas remains.
Using oil or grease on oxygen fittings: oxygen makes these burn fiercely, so oxygen service cleaning is mandatory.
Confusing diluter-demand with pressure-demand: a diluter-demand regulator mixes cabin air at low altitude; a pressure-demand regulator supplies oxygen above cabin pressure.
Assuming a chemical generator can be switched off: once the sodium chlorate candle starts, it supplies oxygen until it is finished.
Mixing up passenger and crew masks: passenger masks are usually continuous-flow and drop automatically; crew masks are usually pressure-demand.

quiz.q: Define hypoxia and time of useful consciousness.
quiz.a: Hypoxia is a shortage of oxygen reaching body tissues. Time of useful consciousness is the time from oxygen loss to inability to act correctly.

quiz.q: Why does a diluter-demand regulator mix cabin air with oxygen at low cabin altitude?
quiz.a: At low cabin altitude the ambient partial pressure of oxygen is enough for the body. Mixing cabin air with oxygen saves stored oxygen and still gives the required partial pressure. As cabin altitude rises, the regulator increases the oxygen fraction and goes to pure oxygen.

quiz.q: A 40 L water-volume cylinder is at 150 bar. Ten passengers each use 5 L/min at 1 bar. Find the gas available at 1 bar and the duration.
quiz.a: Gas available = 40 L × 150 bar ÷ 1 bar = 6000 L. Total flow = 10 × 5 L/min = 50 L/min. Duration = 6000 L ÷ 50 L/min = 120 min.

quiz.q: Crew masks are pressure-demand, passenger masks are continuous-flow. Give one operational reason for each choice.
quiz.a: A pressure-demand crew mask keeps a positive seal and gives oxygen above cabin pressure during rapid decompression or smoke, when the crew must stay alert. A continuous-flow passenger mask is simple, cheap, needs no inhalation valve and lets many passengers share a supply; the crew assists those who cannot pull the mask.

quiz.q: What is a sodium chlorate candle?
quiz.a: A chemical oxygen generator. It burns a sodium chlorate mixture to release oxygen for masks, and once started it cannot be stopped.

quiz.q: Why must oxygen system fittings be free of grease and oil?
quiz.a: Oxygen makes grease and oil burn fiercely. A small amount of oil in a high-pressure oxygen fitting can ignite and cause a fire or explosion, so oxygen service cleaning is required.

quiz.q: A chemical oxygen generator has started. Can the crew stop the oxygen flow by closing a valve? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The candle produces oxygen by a chemical reaction and has no shut-off valve in the generator. The crew can only remove the mask or isolate the affected supply line if the installation provides one; the generator itself runs until the candle is finished.

quiz.q: At 35,000 ft the ambient pressure is 0.24 bar. Oxygen fraction is 0.21. Find P<sub>O2</sub> and compare with sea level, where P<sub>amb</sub> is 1.013 bar.
quiz.a: At 35,000 ft: P<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 0.24 bar = 0.0504 bar. At sea level: P<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 1.013 bar = 0.21273 bar. The high-altitude value is about one quarter of the sea-level value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Military OBOGS uses a zeolite molecular sieve to adsorb nitrogen from bleed air and leave oxygen-rich gas; the sieve beds alternate between production and purge. Newer civil designs use electronic pulse-demand portable oxygen to save gas for walk-around crew. Research looks at lighter composite cylinders and oxygen concentrators for long-endurance aircraft.
